reviews.fact_before: an aquatic animal requires great amounts of water to survive
reviews.correction: An aquatic animal needs a habitat with conditions suitable for its species. The amount of water alone does not establish suitability: water quality, oxygen, temperature, and access to habitat can matter. Great amounts is not a defined water requirement for every aquatic animal.
reviews.reason: An undefined quantity is treated as a sufficient, universal survival condition.

reviews.fact_before: Sperm had to swim from male to female reproductive organs for fertilization.
reviews.correction: Fertilization involves the union of gametes, but not every organism uses freely swimming sperm. In flowering plants, a pollen tube delivers sperm to the female gametophyte. A statement about swimming sperm must identify the organisms and reproductive context before it is applied.
reviews.reason: The past-tense source statement has lost its organism scope and is mixed with unrelated human and plant reproductive claims.

reviews.fact_before: Fertilization occurs when sperm swim to an egg inside an archegonium.
reviews.correction: In ferns, swimming sperm can reach an egg within an archegonium of the gametophyte. An archegonium is a plant reproductive structure; it is not a human uterus and this description is not a universal account of fertilization or pregnancy.
reviews.reason: A plant reproductive structure is incorrectly mixed with human pregnancy and generalized across organisms.

reviews.fact_before: Marine species live mainly in shallow coastal waters.
reviews.correction: Marine species occupy diverse ocean habitats, including deep water. Being marine does not by itself establish that a particular species lives in shallow, warm, or coastal water. Claims about where most species live require a defined population and evidence.
reviews.reason: A broad habitat statement is used to assign habitats to individual species and even to organisms in general.

reviews.fact_before: Roots have primary and secondary meristems for growth in length and width.
reviews.correction: Root apical meristems support primary growth in length. Secondary thickening occurs in plants with the relevant lateral meristems, but typical vascular-cambium secondary growth is not a universal feature of all roots; most monocots lack it.
reviews.reason: The source generalizes one growth pattern to all roots and conflates root growth with shoot branching.

reviews.fact_before: Corals form large colonies in shallow tropical water.
reviews.correction: Many tropical reef-building corals form colonies in shallow warm water. Other corals live in cold, deep water. The habitat of a particular coral must not be inferred solely from the word coral, and a statement about some coral colonies does not apply to every colony-forming animal.
reviews.reason: The scope of tropical reef-building corals is omitted and the property is transferred to other groups.

reviews.fact_before: Most invertebrates have a more complex nervous system.
reviews.correction: More complex requires a comparison group and a defined feature of the nervous system. This record names neither. The label invertebrate alone cannot establish which of two animals has a more complex nervous system or whether most have a particular kind of brain.
reviews.reason: The missing comparison is used to infer unrelated superlatives and brain capabilities.
references: Original supplied QASC fact and its linked records; original source bytes and complete reasoning preserved in immutable source metadata.

reviews.fact_before: Mollusks have a circulatory system with one or two hearts that pump blood.
reviews.correction: Mollusks do not all have one or two hearts. Squid and octopuses have three hearts: two supply the gills and one circulates oxygenated blood to the rest of the body. Heart number must be checked for the particular mollusk group.
reviews.reason: The incorrect generalization explicitly produces a false heart-count claim for squid.

reviews.fact_before: Cells are the microscopic building blocks of organisms.
reviews.correction: Cells are the basic units of organisms, and most are microscopic. Some individual cells, including the bacterium Thiomargarita magnifica, are visible without a microscope. Being a cellular building block does not mean a cell is itself a single molecule.
reviews.reason: An elementary size generalization is treated as absolute and is also misused to equate cells with organic molecules.
